newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asia stocks little changed after Fed rate hike.
newsitem.headline: Asia stocks little changed after Fed rate hike.

text.p: Stocks ended with modest gains throughout most of Asia on Wednesday as traders focused on domestic developments rather than overnight news of a widely anticipated hike in U.S. interest rates, the first in two years.

Hong Kong stocks proved the exception, with the Hang Seng Index shedding 56.14 points, or 0.44 percent, to close at 12,776.39, as local banks followed the move by the Federal Reserve and raised interest rates.
Despite a buoyant property market, Hong Kong dealers said they were wary of pushing the market too high ahead of a long holiday weekend.
"If good pre-sales and land auctions won't drive the market, then we're running into a situation whereby what will?" said James Osborne, sales director at ING Barings.

The Fed's decision to raise the key federal funds rate 1/4 percentage point to 5.50 percent prompted modest losses on Wall Street, which had rallied over 100 points on Monday in anticipation of the move.
The Fed said it took the action to ensure continued steady growth in a low-inflation environment.

Although the modest increase was already being reflected in interest rates and stock prices, traders said there was growing appehension that the U.S. central bank may find cause to push rates still higher later this year.
They said the market will be focused in particular on the U.S. March employment figures due out April 4.
Asian markets opted for a longer-term view of what the Fed may do and took their cues from a spate of local developments.
Shares in Tokyo see-sawed for most of the session before tacking on 32.84 points, or 0.18 percent, to end at 18,472.45.
The market had already discounted the Fed's action and managed to recovery slightly from the sharp selloff that followed a raid at Nomura Securities, Japan's largest broker.

"There does not seem to be much confidence for the new business year and investors are not in a hurry to build positions," Yasuo Ueki, general manager at Nikko Securities, said of the business year that begins April 1.

South Korean stocks, which have been battered by a variety of financial scandals recently, closed sharply higher on a technical rebound coupled with renewed hopes for an early rise in a ceiling on foreign ownership.
The composite stock index jumped 17.72 points, or 2.77 percent, at close at 656.62.
Bargain hunting also propelled Taiwan stocks higher throughout the session, as traders defied a farm crisis and liquidity tightening measures by the central bank.
The benchmark stock index ended 185.90 points, or 2.37 percent, higher at 8,029.33.
Taiwan stocks had lost over 600 points in the four previous sessions in response to a deadly hog disease that forced a halt to billions of dollars worth of pork exports.
Philippine stocks ended higher, with the main index up 19.02 points, or 0.59 percent, at 3,223.14.
Malaysian stocks closed 8.25 points, or 0.68 percent, higher at 1,225.59, while those in Singapore finished up 11.65 points, or 0.55 percent, at 2,111.60.
Indonesian shares rose 2.07 points, or 0.31 percent, to close at 659.35 points. Thai stocks closed 3.61 points higher at 714.29.
Australia's All Ordinaries Index ended up 0.9 points, or 0.04 percent, at 2,404.3, while New Zealand shares closed up 0.60 points, or 0.03 percent, at 2,220.87.
